summary: For children aged 6–8: they need light in order to see, and dark is the absence of light (not a substance). The threshold insight is overturning the intuition that we can see in the dark once our eyes 'get used to it' — for this specific misconception the shift comes most directly from experiencing true darkness, not from being told. A hands-on dark-den/blackout experience (predict → observe → explain) carries the core teaching; a dimmable scene lets the disappearance be run repeatedly on demand; sorting luminous vs non-luminous objects then serves as an end-check that assesses the conclusion. Mastery here is observational (we need light to see); the full source→object→eye light-path model is built later.
misconceptions: Humans can see in the dark once their eyes adjust (the central Oak-flagged misconception: people can see with a little light but not with none).
Darkness is a thing in its own right — 'blackness' is a kind of light or substance — rather than simply the absence of light.
All objects we can see make their own light (failing to separate sources from reflectors).
Only hot or bright objects give out light.
Eyes can 'reach out' and see objects without light (an early form of the extramission idea built on later).

activities.title: Dark den: does the light leave, or the dark arrive?
steps: Before the light goes out, predict aloud what you will see: will the objects slowly appear if you wait, or vanish? Say why first.
Sit in a carefully planned, as-dark-as-possible den/blackout tent with everyday objects — a teddy, a book, a cup — and a small torch or lamp nearby, under adult supervision.

With the light off, notice whether you can see the objects. If the den is truly dark you cannot see them at all; if you can see them faintly, hunt for where a little light is getting in. Name what else you can tell using touch and hearing.
Turn on a small light and watch the objects reappear; describe what actually happened versus your prediction.
Sweep a torch beam around and report which objects become visible — mainly the ones the beam reaches (light bouncing off nearby walls may light others faintly).
activities.insight: We can only see objects when light reaches them and our eyes; in genuine darkness there is nothing to see no matter how long we wait. The teddy did not leave — the light did. Dark is light that is absent, not a thing that arrived.

activities.title: Dimmable scene: run the disappearance yourself
steps: Look at a cosy bedroom scene with a brightness control (a slider or a light-switch, optionally with a torch).
Predict what will happen to each object as you lower the light, then slowly drag the brightness down to zero.
Notice which things fade and vanish (the teddy, book, cup) and which one still glows in the dark (a switched-on screen or night-light that stays on) because it makes its own light.
Flick on the torch and sweep its cone around; report that only objects the beam reaches pop back into view while everything outside the cone stays invisible.
Run the dimming several times to confirm the same thing happens each time.
activities.insight: Lowering the light makes non-luminous objects disappear even though they are still there, while a light source stays visible in the dark. Light must reach an object for it to be seen.

activities.title: Sort: makes its own light vs needs light to be seen
steps: Take a mixed set of objects — lamp, screen, glow-stick, torch (sources); teddy, book, spoon, a mirror, the Moon (non-sources/reflectors).
Sort each into 'makes its own light' or 'only seen when light reaches it'.
Use a lights-off test: in a dark space, which objects still show (switched-on or glowing sources) and which disappear? Remember a lamp, torch or screen makes light only while it is switched on.
Decide where the Moon goes and explain: it is visible because it bounces light from the Sun, so it does not make its own light.
Say in your own words what you need in order to see any of the objects that do not make their own light.
activities.insight: Some objects give off their own light (sources); most objects we see only reflect light that reaches them. Being bright or shiny does not make something a light source.

activities.title: Talk-it-through: scooping out the dark
steps: Discuss: 'If darkness were really a thing, could you scoop it out of the room with a cup? So what actually makes the dark go away?'
Answer whether the Moon is a light source or only bounces light from somewhere else.
A friend says 'I can see a bit in my bedroom at night.' Work out where that little bit of light might be sneaking in from.
State in your own words why a truly light-tight room stays invisible no matter how long you wait.
activities.insight: You add light to make the dark go away; you do not remove a substance. Eyes really do become more sensitive after a while, so in a real bedroom where a little light gets in you can see more over time; but true darkness leaves nothing to see.

checkQuestion: Imagine a room with NO light at all — every window sealed, every crack blocked, completely dark. You sit inside for a long, long time. Can you see the toys in the room if you just wait long enough for your eyes to get used to the dark? Tell me what you think and why.
checkAnswer: No. In complete darkness there is no light at all, so there is nothing to see no matter how long you wait. You can only see when some light reaches the objects and your eyes.
